summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31.1965 and March 31., 1966) in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. The respondent assessee was assessing to wealth Tax for the first assessment years 1966 66, 1967 67 and 1968 68 (both valuation dates). In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued standing interest on it could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal rejected this contention and, in further appeal, held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and accordingly, by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972, it dismissed the appeals. In the reference under s.27(1) of the Act, the assessee contended: (i) that as there maintained its book of account, in accordance therewith, as the cash method of accounting, accrued interest thereon on the monies lending investments could not therefore be included; and (ii) that the Wealth tax Officer was justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis. The Wealth Tax officer sought support from a judgment of this Court in Veda Vedrevu Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax (AIR 1964 SC 264), and the Calcutta High Court in A. T. Mirji vs Commissioner, of Wealth Tax (AIR 1965 C.R. 264), held that even though accounts of the assessees were maintained on cash basis interest due to accrual basis, though not realised, on the outstandings of the money lent business were liable to be included. Since the Appellate Tribunal did not accept this contention, the High Court directed deletion of the additions made by it with respect to the deductions made in its assessment assessment assessments of the assesses. In doing so, the Assessment Officer followed "Commissioner" of Wealth ' Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) (ecidedly an Income Tax Officer. On appeal by the Revenue to this Court it was contended: The provisions contained in section 27(1)(2) of Wealth Act indicate that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last day of the 'previous year", as defined under the Income Tax Act, as "the valuation date". The figure of net wealth, on a legal plane, could be included within the assets of an assessee under the WealthTax Act. Allowing the Appeals, HELD: 1.1 The assets are not confined to cash.

There then started an enquiry followed by departmental proceedings against three persons includ ing the respondent herein. The Personnel Officer of the 23 BSL Project was appointed as Inquiry Officer. The enqui ry was conducted under the Punjab Govern ment Servants Condu t ary Rules 1966. The Enquiry Officer framed charges against the respond ents in the following terms: "That the said Shri Parma Nand, while working as Time Keeper, in time Keeping Sub Division of Beas surplus at Sundernagar during the month of May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar Token N o. 59 T, at serial No. 10 on pages 2 of the relevant pay roll. In view of the above, it cannot be termed th at that the finding returned by the Inquiry Officer is without a ny evidence. This is how the Tribunal dealt with that que s tion: "Lastly, it was argued on behalf of the applicant that t he punishment awarded to him is disproportionate to the charges proved against him and is in stark contrast to the punishment awarded aga bent ly of the charge com por ating to his other three colleagues in whose case only future increments were stopped, the maxi mum being for three years in respect of Shri Sain Ditt a, Clerk. An appreciation of the evidence as done by the witnesses would sh ow that the applicant had entered t he name of Shri Parna Nand in the pay roll for May1969 and so far as other colleagues against him is concerned it is mostly of a circumstanti al nature. There was no direct or expert evidence that it was he who had marked the appearance of Shri The Tribunal, therefore, held that he could not be said to have acted witha ciples in violation of principles of natural justice, and imposed a lesser penalty on him. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf Of th e respondent that if the enquiry held against the delinquent offi cer was proper t the order of the Governor on whose powers by the rules no restrictions in determining the appropriate punishment are placed, w as final, and the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty. Dismissing the appeal and setting aside the order, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was not concerned to decide whether the punishment imposed, provided it is just i fied by the Rules, is appropriate having regard to t he misdemeanour established. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings of the Appella nal Officer or the competent authority are based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [35B C] 2.

The appellant plaintiff instituted a suit in 1968 for a declaration and an injunction restraining the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that he was no more in posses sion of the suit property and that since he had not been dispossessed,in accordance with law, the defen dant plaintiffs who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted therefrom. Both sides contended before the trial court that defendant No 1 was a trespasser in the property and was liable to eviction, and that he should have let out the property to defendant Nos. 2 and hence, it was not entitled for any such possession. The trial court upheld the contention of the defant plaintiffs that the suit was barred by res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that: (1) on the expiry of the lease period at the end of December 1967 the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and defendant No 2 was, therefore, entitled to let out his property to him; and (2) since he was not in de facto possession no injunction could be granted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The suit was maintainable in view of Order 2 rule 2(1)(d) of Civil Proce dure Act, 1908, as the plaintiff had not challenged the correctness or contrary to the decree passed by the trial Court on Mat ch Ch Ch Thota Ava vs Gopal Bapuji. (b) Under section 7 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a court shall have jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1025G] 1022 2(a). In case of threatened wrongful possession section 8A says that any tenant in possession of any land or dwelling house who apprehends that he may be dispossessed contrary to his provisions of the Act may apply in writing for such possession to the Mamlatdar for an order safeguarding his right to possession. Within this period, one of the duties and functions to be performed by the tricts under the Act is the Mamlatdar: (i) whether any person is a tenant or should be deemed to be a tenant under the Bombay Act; and, (ii) whether the tenancy of any deemed tenant is legally terminated and if no, whether the tenant evicted from the land held by him as such is entitled to restoration of possession. [ 1025C] 3(b). Section 7 provides that a person entitled to more than one relief in respect of the same cause of action may sue for all or any of them; but if he omits, except with the leave of the court, to sue for every such reliefs he shall not afterwards sue for any relief so omitted. [1007C] (c) The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 read with section 58(2) and specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle. decide questions such as : (i).

The petitioners are engaged as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the ' Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32, they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". The peti tioners in the writ petition sought the enforcement of the aforesaid fundamental right on the ground that they want the same pay of the regular employees as carpti ters or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also sought regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The Corporation resisted the claim and contended that the petitioners were employed by a Company incorporated under the . They cannot enforce the right to equal pay for Equal work. The claim was contested by the Corporation contending that the Corpora tion has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. Allowing the writ Petition, the Court, HELD: 1.1 In the first place, even assum ing that the Petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts in the Government service, the petitioners cannot enforce their right to "equal Pay for equal pay". The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts or in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by it. Unless it is shown that there is a discriminat ing amongst the same set of employees by the two different master in the same establishment, the principle of "equal wages for equal Work" cannot be enforced. [669C E] 2.2 In the second place, the petitioner in the first instance, even as a worker constable in the Delhi Police Force under the Delhi Administration, cannot enforce his right to 'equal pay. The discrimination alleged must be beyond the same standard of discrimination pleaded by the petitioners and is rejected. The Court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences, ; , followed.

Section 52 of the Indian , as amended by Act VI of 1929, provided that in order to enable a testator to make certain dispositions about his property I have no doubt that he has given authority to it. Section 52 Of the , which was inserted into the , required that the testator had the knowledge of the contents of the will. The appellant along with her two daughters and daughters filed a suit claiming a declaration that the said properties would vest in them by a will. It was alleged, inter alia, on behalf of her husband that the will was executed by his duly authorised agent who was incapable of making any statement about their contents and that at the material time Lakshmamma was not in a sound disposing state of mind or that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intention. The trial court held that the execution of the trust deed did not disclose that the executant had the know ed, powers of attorney she had. It further held that there was no evidence in rebuttal led by respondent 1 regarding the instructions given by Lakshmma to him 56 in the matter of the execution. On a reference, the High Court held (i) it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature on the instrument intending that the recitals and the dispositions in the will should be executed; (ii) there was also no evidence to show satisfactorily as to what happened on the day when he attested the will, this witness had frankly stated that he could not state definitely whether the whole of the document was read over to the testatrix before he put it signifying his signature to the said Will. Held, further, that the onus was heavy on the propounder and unless there were any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution, the burden was heavy upon him to remove such legitimate doubts in the case.

Section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 empowers the Central Government to enhance or reduce the rate of royalty prescribed by the Second Schedule in respect of any mineral subject to the condition that the Central Govern ment shall not enhance the rate Of royalty in respect thereof. The Act was passed in the year 1957 by Parliament to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. Under section 3A of the Act, the words 'minerals ' were defined as including all minerals except mineral oils. Clause (e) of the said section defines minor minerals ' as building stones etc., gravel, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposes and any other mineral which the Central Govt may by notification in the Official Gazette declare to be a minor mineral. The petitioners challenged the validity of Rule 21 on various grounds, namely: 1. that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State the levy is bad; and 2. that in any event the impugned notification was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The impugned Rule 21 which was substituted in the place of the former rule 21 was invalid as it was discriminatory in character. [415G] (b). In view of the decision of this Court in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and ors., ; , the validity Of the Rules made thereunder had been considered and the contentions urged by them against the said rule in those petitions, had been rejected in the present case. [413G] The levy is ex ceived under a law made by the Central Gov ernment on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 304(b) applies. It is not an imposition made by a law or by the authority on which it alone the restrictions contemplat ing under Article 709 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [414B] (c). The levy in question is ex facie ordo ned and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. The burden of establishing that the levy was unreasonably heavy, is on the petitioners. It can be urged that the impugned Rule is challeng ing the power or the power which has been conferred by it. [416C] (d). Section 15 of Part II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution does not authorise the State Government to show such con tention while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. The levy was arbitrarily imposed. It was obvious that the petitioners were lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes of business and that the royalties in question are ultimately passed on to the consumers. It cannot be said that the business is adversely affected in such a way that it is liable to be struck down on the ground of arbitrariness. [411C E] In the instant case, the levy in questo nent to show concession while promulging the Rules does not specifically authorise the state Government to make such discrimination. The power exercised is legislative in character and the authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make rules equi table by necessary implication.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the trusteeship of the temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship were hereditary trustees because their office devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is specifically provided for by the founder on condition that the scheme of such succession is still in force. The Commissioner held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" since their office fell under section 6(9) of the Madras Act 1 of 1925, and therefore in view of section 6 (9) the Commissioner must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section. HELD: The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interest in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". A person cannot succeed to his own office. In Black 's Law Dictionary, the word "reactful" is defined as follows: "The revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution." (4) The right by which one set of men may acquire ,a property in all the goods, movables, and other chattels of a corporation. Further the appellant could succeed to the office of trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of one year and not for life. [445 H; 428 A B] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , applied.

The deceased, Execution of a charge sheet against the appellant and two other accused by absconding accused, was committed to the Sessions Court on April 26, 1971,, against the present appellant without the absconding accused. The prosecution case against him was that on the last day when his brother was sleeping in the open space he was running a fire at him with knife. He further saw his two brothers and R committing murder. The trial court acquitted the second accused. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted the appellant 's second accused, whose conviction was also upheld by the High Courts. Hence this appeal. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1. There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the site plan. There were also no blood stains on the bench where he was said to be sleeping. The crowd had gathered at the place of occurrence already when a little earlier than PW 4, did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. It is difficult to accept this explanation of this witness. Assuming that his earlier version in the first information report is true that the deceased chased the accused as the latter was running away after the assault, there is hardly any corroboration of his testimony. [701 B C; 712 A] 2. The High Court was not even right in convicting the second respondent on the sole testimony of a solitary eye witness for convicting the accused facing a murder charge. [ 712 D E] 3. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the court while appreciating ocular testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other.

A firm of solicitors was dissolved and the partnership was carried on. The firm kept its accounts with the assessee. At the time of his death there was a credit made by the deceased to the company of a sum representing the outstanding professional fee earned by him prior to the discontinuance of their practice but realised it during the Calendar year which was the previous year. Held, that in order that a person died during the previous and was assessed under section 24 B of the Income tax Act if he had not died his legal personality ceased on his death and the income received by him before his death should be deemed to have been received by the dead person and therefore the income for which it was taxed must be held not to be liable to tax in the several years of assessment. An individual assessee has ordinarily to be a living person and there can be no assessment on a dead person. The individual assessee had ordinarily to he a living man, and there could be no assessment on a deceased person and the assessment was a charge in respect of income of the previous years and not a charge or in respect for the income of that year as measured by the income Of the previous Company. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs E. Alfred, , applied. The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B and cannot be extended beyond the object for which the it was enacted. A taxing statute is considered not with a narrow or restricted purpose but with a broad and liberal construction. For the purposes of assessment under assessment under that Act only those properties are liable to be taxed as income, and the assessee has been rightly assessed by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of such assessment all the substantive provisions of section 23B do not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased 's property beyond the previous or the account year in which the person died, or for that purpose he had no assets.

The petitioners were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. Under section 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, the Government declared that everyone had been appointed directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved by the State Public Employment Order, 1957. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds: (i) that the Constitution was speaking of State and Union territory; (ii) that it was not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid or not. HELD : (i)(a) The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. [117A] (b) Section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957 does not employ the words "any requirement" and therefore section 3 of . is ultra vires the Constitution. [118C] (c) The scope of the freedom of employment guaranteed in article 16 was well settled by this Court as the words 'residence within the State or Union territory ' which words mean what they say, neither more nor less. It follows that section 3 does not use the word 'state '. Section 3 does no doubt provide an inclusive definition of residence within the meaning of the expression 'State and Union territories ' which mean what it says, neither less than. It is a matter for creation of residential qualification for employment and it is not necessary that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns or villages. [119G H; 120A C] (d) The argument of Mr. Das that Parliament can make a provision regarding residence in any particular part of State would render the general prohibition lose all its meaning and the words used control within it by making a declaration and leaving the details to be filled in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments, is valid.

The appellant was charged with having committed offences under sections 52 and 53 of the Post Office Act, 1898. The Sessions Judge acquitted two of them. One of the reasons given by him for setting aside his acquittal was that on behalf of the prosecution the evidence regarding seizure was not produced. It was contended for the State (1) that the appellant had an opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilised the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession; (2) that it would not be correct to say that the five registered letters were secreted by the appellant, and (3) that in examining the appellant the Sessions Court did not comply with the requirements of section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held:(i) The language of section 53 of an Act is theft. Ordinarily it cannot be contended that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Indian Post Office ' Act, but where the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If, therefore, it was the intention of the legislature that for an officer of the post office to be punished for secreting, destroying or throwing away a postal article in the oucrse of transmission by post the entrustment would be theft but the Act which runs thus states that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed to be in course of transmission.

The appellants were alleged to have been abused and threatened by the Respondent that he should be laboured and his property worth about Rs. 40/ which was damaged. On September 2, 1963, the respondent filed an application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 against the appellants and section K. Srivastava for being impleaded as a party to the writ petition in the High Court. The High Court stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat but on December 23, 1963 a notice was issued to the five members of that Bench to assemble on December 25, 1963 and they were heard by the respondent, who refused to take it. This fact was denied and the High court held that the respondent had knowledge of the order and that the order was passed deliberately to pass it to pass the order of the High 'Court. In appeal by special leave: HELD: (i) The High High Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Pan chachas to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the application before him. At any rate he had apparently no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before them. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn it, he cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120 F G; 120 B D E] (ii)The High Court while dealing with the evidence had not kept in mind the principles which we have mentioned above.

The appellant was tried under section 302, I.P.C., and sentenced to death for the murder of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge accepted the prosecution case and convicted and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for life. The High Court however did not rely on this extra judicial confession. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a police officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that he had purchased a sword in the Canal at the Police Station. 208 Dismissing the appeal, HELD: An extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. [208B C] In the instant case, the extrajudicial confession was not admissible as it purported to be a confession made by the appellants to Ujagar Singh and consequently the High 's view that there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh 's statement regarding the appellant 's confessing to him that he did commit the murder was wrongly rejected by the Court. [209E F] The extra judicial confessional confession of appellants to 489 Ujagar Singh found ample support from the facts that the accused had a motive to harm Sheo Sahai and that it was not a matter of surprise that he should have made a statement that he bad committed the murder, to which the evidence of the appellant and having been awarded the proper sentence. [210 E] In view of the well settled position in criminal appeals by special Leave the Supreme Court rightly held that there was good reasons in convicting the accused appellants for offences under section I. P.C. and had been awarded a particular sentence. The extrajudicial confessional confession made to the accused appellant to Ujagar singh found ample strength from the reasons given by the courts below and also considered it for reasons given, not to justify the rejection of the statements of the accused at the police Station.

% The respondents in c.A. 1640/79 challenged the electoral roll of the appellants by way of an election petition before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 requesting the court to make an order quashing the electoral rolls and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the election and directing the respondent not to notify the results of the Election under Rule 46 of the Rules pending disposal of the writ petition. A Division Bench of the High court dismissed the petition holding (i) that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation Act, 1956; and (ii) that even though an assessment was made by the Deputy Collector with regard to the irregularity in the division of Raipur town into different wards for purposes of election. On appeal, this Court by its order dated December 31, 1978 allowed the appeals, setting aside the electoral Roll and directing that the Panchayat Constituency Election Officer shall abide by it expeditiously, which was done on November 16, 1978. In view of the interim order passed in Civil Appeal No. 17/79 before the Supreme Court on January 20, 1979, it took place on December 31.1978 after which the poll had to take place on April 30, 1978 and the poll was held and 44 persons were declared elected. The final electoral roll was published on November 25, 1978 notifying that the poll, if necessary would take place in all the constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the high Court for quashing the elections and directing them to refrain from conducting the poll on December 30,1978. Thereafter the calendar had to be adjourned to December 30 six, 1978 at the request of the counsel for the respondents. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the Writ Petition till December 28. 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under rule 4(i) of Rules entitling them to raise a grievance with regard thereto within a period of 20 days. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding (1) that respondent No. 2, the Deputy Collec tor had asked them to appear before him on October 30, l4 1978 and that as he did not produce any evidence in support of his claim, his application was rejected; and and (2) that inspite of the aforesaid interim order made by this Court, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objections were prevented from preferring them within the 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under rule 46 of tO the Rules within which the claims and objection could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable to be rejected. Allowing the appeals on the ground that since one of the grounds on which the High COurt dismissed the Writ petition was that the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High Courts, this court HELD: 1. The Court is right in doing so, since if it agree with the High ' Court on the question as to whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under article 226 is a matter within the discretion of the high court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to t the surrounding circumstances. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity of an Election to a local authority is challenged.

The respondent company was prosecuted under section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913, for failure to register the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 222(I)(a), alleging that the business of the Company was not being carried on. The High Court however held that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit etc. after it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly did not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In the State 's appeal to this Court against the order of acquittal of directors, HELD: The High Courts had taken a contrary view and followed the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case. They could not ignore the clear words of the section. Where the words of section are very clear it is unnecessary to consider whether it embodies any principle and whether that principle is consistent with the principle as embodied a certain other sections which are differently worded. In interpreting a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of a section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions Of law requires that this section should be interpreted is the same way. [422 H] The Court observed: " If it were the case that everything required to be inserted in the list was dependent on the fact of the general meeting having been held, it might perhaps have been contended with some force that it is impossible to say what day is the fourteenth day thereafter. This observation may provide no defence to a prosecution under section 133 but it might well do so in a prosecution u/s 134.

The respondent was tried by a Special Court for offences alleged to have been committed on his house and that he was convicted of the offence under section 3 of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. The High Court quashed the conviction holding not only that section 5(1) of the Act was ultra vires the Constitution only so far as it authorised the State Government to direct that certain offences or classes of cases should be tried by the Special Court; but also that the classification must not be arbitrary and must be rational. Held, that section 6 (1) was valid as it gave unguided power to the State Govern ment to direct "cases" to be tried in any district for trial of specified offences. Where the statute provided that a person may be convicted of an offence disclosed by the evidence as having been committed by him even though he was not charged with it and it happens to be a more serious offence, the court might interfere under article 136, if there had been discrimination between persons found in the evidence or materials which were to be considered together in full. Held also, further, that while section 5 of the impugned Act could have no application to cases under section 5 (1), inasmuch as it empowered the State government to direct a particular case to be mentioned by its own judgment, there was no discrimination at all in the exercise of its power if it was otherwise in good faith and in either case the resulting discrimination will both prejudice the accused or would lead to denial of equality before law. Held further, also, that in cases like these, special treatment made to "cases", is reasonable, as compared with other offences and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to the object of the legislation. [219 H] The classification must be based on some intelligible differentia which are to be found in all persons grouped together and not in others who are left out but those qualities or characteristics must have a reasonable relation to that object of legislation. Where an Act does not state what exactly were the offences which in its opinion need a speedier trial and why it is so considered, a mere statement in general terms of the object sought to be achieved cannot mean that if the Act did not state precisely what are the offences in its di rect, that would be for the good of the people and substitute their individual and personal opinions for that of the government of the day, or that they may usurp the functions of the legislature. [205 C D] If the Act does so, it can be said to have violated the equality clause, though questions relating to proper exercise of such power or the limits of delegation might arise, as distinguished from classes of offences or categories of cases. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", 'classes of offences ' and "classes Of cases" for the purpose of being tried by Special Court. The Act could therefore be saved on the evidence which it had founded.

The Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966, envisaged categorization of personnel manning the service into five different categories viz. Categories 'A to 'E '. Rule 5 provided for the authorized permanent and temporary strength of the Service. Under r.4, the controlling authority had power to interchange any post included in the senior scale without altering the authorized strength in each category. R.8 provided for 100% of the vacancies in Category 'B ' of the supertime scale were to be filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the post in the junior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of vacancies thereof were to he filled by direct recruitment in the manner prescribed in the Second Schedule. By a Notification dated January 1, 1965, the initial appointments were notified. The essential pre condition for the inclusion of a post in a Central Health service was that a medical qualification recognised under the Indian Medical Council should be prescribed for it. By the Central Heath Service ( Amendment) Rules 1966, the Central Health Services (Amendment & Validation) Rules were framed which came into force on May 5, 1963. R8 provided that every vacancy in the Specialists ' Grade shall be filled up by promotion of General Duty Officers Grade I and Specialists Grade Officers in the ratio of 2 : 3 on the basis of merit and seniority and the remaining 50% of t vacancies are to be carried by direct Recruitment in the way prescribed in a second schedule. By another notification dated January 17, 1976 the initial appointment were notified, but the essential pre conditions for inclusion of candidates in the First Schedule were that a Medical qualification recognised followed under the Punjab Health Service was that that a post doctor should be in the line of and eligible to be appointed as Professor or Associate Professor in the concerned speciality in a medical college/teaching institution. Rule 4 provided for promotion by promotion from General Duty officers Grade I, possessing the qualifications and experience prescribed in Annexure 1 to the Second schedule. Rule 6 provided that 50% vacancies in the Supertime scale shall be reserved for promotion through departmental promotion Committee of Officers holding the posts in the Senior Scale with gazetted pay. 8 (2A) provided that if no suitable officer is available for appointment to the post of Associate Professor or Assistant Professor in any medical college or teaching institution from the Grades of Assistant Professor or Lecturer, as the case may be, such vacancy shall be carried forward by direct recruit in the time specified in the second schedule, and that if the no suitable Officer is available the appointment shall be made. By an order dated January 9, 1974 the Central Government appointed a Selection Committee to recommend the name of the appellant for promotion to the next higher post under r. 6. The Selection Committee fixed the inter se seniority of the members of the Selection Committee who were to rank senior to the appellant as well as by the Punjab Public Service Commission. The appellant was not only holding the Post of Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital but was also personally associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy (ex officio) in the Medical College, Rohtak, and he did not appear for the interview. The Government of India by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Director of Medical Education that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist. The Ministry of Health was of the view that although the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for teaching post the teaching experience gained by him while holding the position of Assistant Surgeon cum Associate Professor (exRetd officio) which the appellant held in the 95th of October, 1964 cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of determining the question of his eligibility for appointment as Professor/ Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College.

An industrial dispute between the workmen and the management of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., was referred by the State Government under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Tribunal enumerating 30 different items of dispute. The Tribunal gave its award on all the thirty items. The special leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. In appeal it was contended that even in adopting the latter course, the Tribunal committed an error inasmuch as, in making the calculation, the Court only tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living consequent on such revision. It was urged by counsel for the workmen that casual workers should also be paid minimum wages on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum wage was fixed by the order of the Tribunal which is being varied by this time, a period of 5 to 6 years has elapsed, so that the Company would have to pay arrears of wages for this long period. On behalf of the workmen it was argued, inter alia, that in fixing the minimum wages according to the Coal Award, the principle of fixation of wages on basis of Comparison in the region laid down in the French Motor Car Co., was not rigid and so the Tribunal had committed an errato nal error inasmuch, the gross violation of article 14 or 16 of the Constitution. HELD : The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950 provides that where a particular concern is already paying the highest wages in its own line of business, the industrial courts would be justified in looking at wages paid in that region in other lines of business. It should take care to see that the concerns from other lines Of business taken into account are such as are nearly similar as possible to the line of employment carried on by the concern before it. The principle which is applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into consideration. The argument that the Tribunal has committed an mistake at this stage cannot be accepted because the tribunal had, based its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there was no justification to introduce a new element of payment of bonus to casual and badi workers at this Stage. [671G H] French Motor Company Ltd., Dwarka Cement Works, Dwarka vs Its Workmen ; , followed. In giving its decision, left it to the workmen to ask for increase in minimum wage on any further rise in wages, in case there is marked variation in the Price Index, and, in no ease is the Dearness allowance taken out into account. There can be no doubt that in an industrial dispute which relates to wages by a company, there can be such linking so as to bring in continuous variation of the wage depending on the variation in price Index. It is not necessary that the minimum. wage should have been fixed by it at the average level of wages in the other comparable industries in the same region, namely, the three Collieries, the Rourkela Steel Plant and the Cement Factory. In the present case, such a principle would justify an adjustment by granting bonus to workmen who are being paid production bonus is one of two aspects which should be taken into scrutinise for ascertaining if there was any justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average minimum wage payable by those industries. [672C D] French Car Co. (India) Ltd., vs Its Workers ; , relied on. The arbitrator, in giving its award, held that it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for these Paper Mills with that of the Company. It had therefore taken into consider the minimum Wages in these concerns on the basis of the average fixed wages and dearness allowance. [673E G] French car Co. Ltd., ; and Dind Bank of India vs The Workmen, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R.

The assessee filed his income tax return in respect of which the Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. The assessee challenged the validity of that notice before the High Court on various grounds but as there was no material before him which could satisfy the requirements of either cl. (a) or clause (b) of section 147, the Income tax Officer had in consequence of information in his possession reason to believe that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any assessment year. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the assessee against the judgment of the High court on various contentions and hence it was not necessary to examine the other contention advanced on behalf of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : The Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of notice under sections 147 and 151 of the Act. [466C] If only he had read the report carefully, he could never have come to the conclusion on the material before the Commissioner that this is a fit one for the issued of notice. [449E] In the instant case the report submitted by him under section 151(2) does not mention any reason for coming to the finding that it was a suitable case for issue of a notice under s 148, nor could it be said that he as a consequence of ' information in the possession had reasons to believe, that income liable to tax had escaped assessment.

The appellant firm carried on the business of manufacturing and selling yarn and textiles, which were taxed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The question in this appeal was whether the business which had been subjected to tax during the years 1948 49 and 1949 50, taken place before and after that date, was a business carried on by a firm, as a result of a transfer by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948, by the appellant. Held, that where the activity in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25(3) can be obtained, is not a mere change of ownership but a succession not amounting to a mere severance of business, and if it was held that on that ground there was no succession within the meaning of sub section (4), it could not be said that the relief intended for the money lending business which was carried on was by one of the members of the erstwhile family. If this view was correct, the firm was entitled to the benefit mentioned in section 25 (4) only if there had been a succession by virtue of which the provisions of sub s.(4) of section 26 or for the purpose of section 24(2). The business continued in the hands of the same person who had paid tax under the Act of 1918 and was, therefore, not a case in which both the sub sections applied at the same time because, there were changes in the constitution of the partnership. The business which bad been subjected lo tax by the Act Of 1918 even though there were new changes in its constitution.

A partition between the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons, was effected between them in December 1952 and December 1954. The plaintiff 's claim to a share in the coparcenary property which had been divided during his lifetime, as the plaintiff 'S 's self acquisitions and that he had partitioned the properties after his death in 1960, on the basis of that partition having taken place during his life time, there was no joint family in existence between him and his two sons. The Trial Court rejected the defendant 's case that the properties belonged to the joint families consisting of their wives, herself, and their children. The trial court dismissed the suit as barred by limitation. On appeal the High Court held that since the widow and daughter are among the female relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and Khandappa died leaving behind a widow and daughters, the proviso to section 6 came into play and the normal rule is excluded. Allowing the appeal this Court ^ HELD: (1) The mere fact that two interpretations of explanation I were reasonably possible, cannot justify limiting the plaintiff"s share to 1/24th by ignoring the 1/4th share which she would have obtained had there had been a partition during his husband 's life time between him, and his sons. [764 H] (2) The fact that in a partition between Khandappa and his wife the plaintiff has an equal share, the plaintiff landlord 's share therein will be 1/6th, that is to say, 1/25th; and so far as there is no difficulty. [774 A B] (3) The assumption of a fiction created by Explanation I in the manner suggested by the appellant, has to be treated and accepted as a concrete reality, something that cannot be recalled just as a share allotted to a coparcener in an actual partition cannot generally be recalled. The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in interest which the deceased bad in the coparcener 's coparcenary property at the time of his death, in addition to the share which he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition. The allotment of this share is not a processual step devised merely for the purpose of working out some other conclusion.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were promulgated by the Parliament and provided for its management. Clause (2) empowers the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service of any employee of the Corpo ration belonging to Class I or class II categories appointed to the serv ice of the Corpora tion on or after 1st September 1956 which was being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and provides for its re ceipt. On December 20, 1957 the Governor of the State appointed an employee belonging to the Class I & Class II employed in the service even before he attained the age of 60 years. The first respondent joined service in the Corporation after 1.9.1956 and was transferred from place to time in terms of the settlement which followed effect with the effecting com pany of the two settlements. On the passing of the said Regulations, the management of the controlled business of all insurers in India con cerned to nationalise the life insurance busi ness, the Life Insurance Corpora ties in India, however, continued to be carried on till 60 years of age but the employees belonging to class I and Class II who were appointed to Class III posts before 1.11.1958 had to retire on completion of 58 years of service subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. The second respondent joined Service after 1 9.9 1956. On 1st October 1962, a Circular was issued by the Government for the Corporation 's attention to the implementation of the above said Circular. Thereafter, in accordance with the settlement arrived at between the parties, it was agreed that 60 years ' age should be fixed as provided therein. Later on, by another circular issued on 21.1.1977 withdrawing the power to extend the service upto 60 years from 58 years to 58 years on the ground that the employees and agents of the Corporation who were employed after 1 1st Septem ber 1956 had to superannuate on completion Of 58 years came to an end. However, in regard to the retirement age which would be 60 years, the first respondent issued a Circular dated 2nd February 1977 whereby it was provided that if not acceptable to any employee the Corporation might terminate his employ ment by giving him compensation equivalent to three months ' remuneration unless the contract of service with such employee provided for a shorter notice of termination. Thereafter the first and second respondents filed a Writ Petition No. 6849 of 1984 which was allowed on August 17, 1985 taking the view that section 49(2) of the Act is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution since it has substituted the terms and conditions of service applicable to employees of insurers whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it or for the purposes of reducing the remuneration payable to them in such manner as it thought fit and if the alteration was not acceptable, then notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1) of section 11 or in any contract of serv ice, the Central Govern ment might for the purpose of rationalising the pay scales of employees of their insurers whose business had already been transferred by virtue of the settle ment. The High Court found fault with the classification made between the employees falling under clause (b) into two categories namely those employ ees belonging to a company where there was a rule similar to clause (bb) as regards the age and retirement, the employees could continue as long as they were found to be physically and mentally fit, it became necessary to fix the age at which persons would have held the same on the appointed day if the Act had not been passed, and also that the disparity made between those employees of the erstwhile insurers was not arbitrary.

The appellants wrote a letter on 20th February 1975 to the President with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by two members of the Bar Association, who had taken a copy of their letter to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, for the same and they were also given a notice to the appellants to show cause why contempt should not be punished for contempt when the Government passed an order in compliance with the directions given by the Supreme Court. The Advocate General stated that the contents of his letter were incorrect inasmuch as he had offered to the Vice President that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Bar room. A notice was issued by the High Court on 12th March, 1975 as follows: "Letter dated 20th Febru ary, 1975 a copyo of an application dated 23rd February, 1975 signed by 15 members of District Bar Association Bhiwani has been placed for the consideration of this Bench." On a perusal of the contents thereof a prima facie case of criminal contempt is made out. (2) The High COurt proceeded on the basis that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. (3) It was also necessary to state here that if anyone address es on political considerations or disput tions the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The reason is obvious. It is no part of the duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of his office of a Court to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take appropriate action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech.

The petitioners were the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd., a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, for storing and selling jute and Gunn Brokers etc. Their case was that they had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and that had thus evaded taxa tion. The petitions filed by them were heard in the Supreme Court by section M who held that sub section (4) of section 5 conferred a power on the Commission to require any person or banking company to prepare and furnish on or before a specified date written statements of accounts and affairs verified in such manner as may be prescribed by the Commission. He also found that the provisions of sections 5(1), 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 were not repugnant to article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) since section M had held that the investigation must be completed in a reasonable manner it could not be argued that in any case section 5(2) Of the Act violated article 19 (1)(g) because the case of the petitioner was referred to the Commission under the provisions contained in section 5 (1); and (ii) since there was no substantial difference in procedure prescribed by sections 37 and 38 of the Indian Income tax Act and so it could be urged that there was any substantial difference which required consideration in the case. Held: The contention must be negatived. There is a proviso to sub section(4) which says that for the purpose of enabling the person whose case or points in whose case is being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on the record against him, he shall, on application made in this behalf and on payment of such fees as may been prescribed by rules, be furnished with certified copies of documents, statements, papers and materials brought on them by the commission. If any person whose cases are referred to under section 5 contravenes any other law that may be declared invalid without prejudice to any penalty under the Act it would not violate article 20(3) Of 'the Constitution. The procedure thus prescribed by section 34 of the Act is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed in sections 37, 38 and 35 which are dealt with in sub section 4 of section S of the impugned Act.

The main object of the Federation as given in its Memorandum of Association is "regulation of hours of work, payment of wages, leave, holiday, terms of service and other conditions of work of persons employed in shop commercial establishment, establishment for public entertainment or amusement and other establishments and to provide for certain matters connected therewith. " The primary objects of this Federation as stated in its preamble is " regulation of hours work, pay of wages etc." The main object is the establishment of the Association as set forth in its memorandum of association; while the definition of "establishment" includes "shop ' and 'commercial Establishment", the definitions of ' commercial establishment ' and "industry" given in a different statute are mutually exclusive. Further, the definition as well as various other relevant provisions of the Act is material for our purpose. They read "Commercial establishment" means any premises wherein any trade, business or profession or any work in connection with or incidental or ancillary thereto is carried on and includes a society registered under the , and charitable or other trust, whether registered or not, which carries on any business, trade or profession. " Establishment" means a shop as a commercial establishment. Besides, the definitions in section 2(9) and (27) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954 are mutually concurrent. The dictionary meaning of the word 'business ' is that it includes a shop or a factory registered under an Act, a company which carries out any business; but this aspect has to be borne in mind. A person who is carrying on a profession as it does not include a shop within the definition must be deemed to have given an opportunity for doing so and his activities could bring it within the category of "shops ' or "business" within the meaning of section 2 (5). The definition of 'establishment" is wider than that of "commercial establishment". For the application of the provisions of sub sections (5), (9) & (27), the Act, as well in view of this Court 's decision in R. K. Mittal vs State of Delhi, [1971] 1 S.C.R. No. 887, is not applicable to the instant case because the definition given in section2(j) is far wider than the definition under section 2.(9) of .

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, was the owner of certain land. The estate was originally in question and with a view to obtaining education from the Government, the village official of the village went to the village. Later, the State granted a pension of Rs. 36,322/8/ to Babu Har Narain Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur which the amount was fixed at Rs.36,322. The Income tax Officer 's view that though the Government recouping this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appeared in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay it, and since the purpose of these documents falls within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922, and as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of rent collection, the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The sources of the the pension were a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate sources of income were not land or rent collections from land it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of 1922 Act. The source of this pension was a liability undertaking undertaken by it for extinguishing the proprietary rights. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that since the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year, the source of income still remained the arrangement and not land. An appeal filed by the State Government to the Income Tax Tribunal was allowed by the Tribunal. In reference under section 66A(2) of Act the High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collected after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment and that it was not agriculture income. On a reference, the High 'Court held that the source where the allowance or pension was the arrangement arrived at in 1837, then the income could not not be held to be derived from land within the ambit of section 2 (1) (a). Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1(i) Where an owner of an estate exchanges a capital asset for a perpetual annuity it is ordinarily taxable income in his hands. The position will be different if he exchanges (1 ) 30 T.C. II. (2) 30 T .C.II. (3) 707 his estate for a capital sum payable in installments. The installments when received would not be taxable income. [707 D] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Triolu Baliram Narain Rai, and Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa, , relied on. (ii) On the true interpretation of the arrangement, arrived at into 1837 and therefore it was clear that it is not agricultural Income as defined in the Act; but in this case, no material has been produced to show that the allowance varied from years to year. Assuming that the amount varied from ' year to ' year, what the parties call it. [ ameliorating the wording of the document arrived at; it was therefore not agricultural Incometax income as defined under the Act. [ 709 E F] (iii) The respondent did not acquire any interest in land or any land revenue and could not therefore be taxed as agricultural income. There was no material to show, that the allowances were in fact a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assesses 's predecessor in 1838. [700 G] State vs Kunwar Shri Trivi Misra & Anr., [1959] Supp. 2 S.C R. 1054 and M/s.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court set aside a grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and enhanced the number of permits granted to the private operators from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by proviso to section 63(7) and the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the application for permits to be granted, and held that after considering the claims of the eligible applicants in the manner indicated in Sher Singh 's case and examining the merits of the claims, the applications became entitled to be included. It was, therefore, directed that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal should dispose of the applications afresh in accordance with law, after considering all the claims raised by the applicants without waiting for any further appeal, and after giving a personal hearing to the eligible applicant. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation appealed to this Court for relief by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tile State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims Of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. Except in the cases of a specified notified route, the application of no applicant may be altogether excluded from consideration on the sole ground that another applicant is entitled to preference under one or the other provisions of the statute. The proviso to about section 63 (7) specifically provides that other conditions being equal, an application for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating in any interState route shall be given priority over all other applications. While it is true that section 47(1 H) does not expressly refer to "other things being equal", it appears to him, be implicit in the provision that other things are equal. The rule is a rule of caution and if the discretion to grant approval is to be exercised once the minimum conditions are fulfilled. [1015 A C] 2.1 There is no question of eliminating private operators merely because the Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permits under Chapter IV, it must satisfy the Regional Transport Authority that it is better suited than the private operator to render transport facility to the travelling public. The scheme makes no reference to the proviso to Section 63(1).

The respondent, a permanent employee of the appellant State, entered service in the Gondal State in 1927 as a jailor. The State of West Bengal vs Abdul Majid, [1955] 1 S.C R.

The appellant 's predecessor in interest, was granted a mining lease of the coal and coal mining rights in respect of 300 bighas out of his 400 bighas to one P. W. No. 1. When P executed a lease of 1928, I instituted a suit for conversion of property on the northern boundary of P.W. 3(b) from another plot of 96 bighas to another plot. The plaint was based on the following allegations: (a) that the southern boundary of the appellant ' s leasehold is conterminous with the northern boundaries of the respondents ' lease hold; (b) that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines on August 18, 1941, the plaintiff made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. On those allegations, they asked for the following reliefs: (i) That the intermediate boundary line between the appellant and P; and (ii) that a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the appellants ' coal land and cutting and removing coal therefrom. Held, that the suit was for conversion to property and the question of limitation as framed by section 100 of the Indian Evidence Act would not survive in the present case. Under section 101 of the Evidence Act the burden in the former sense is on the party who comes to court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In the instant case, P proved that the knowledge of his father was within three years of the suit and that the entire burden was on the plaintiff in these suits to prove that he obtained the knowledge thereof by examining the school records and having considered the extent of land being thereby unworkable is entirely lost to them for ever. It was not necessary for him to prove this part in the plaint which was beyond three years from the date when they had knowledge of it. Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, (1920) L.R. 59 I.A. 588 and Sundarji Shivji vs Secretary of State for India, [1939] F.C.R., p. 751, relied on. Held further, that in view of the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below in respect to this issue, the court must be held to have acted affirmatively. No other point was raised and it was not a pure question of law involved in the appeal.
