In appeal to this Court, the appellant contended that it was entitled under r., 18 (i) of the Standing Orders to dispense with the service of any employee after complying with its terms, and that, in view of the decisions cited above, the employer could dismiss the employee and defend his action under the r.18 (a), and it was not open to the industrial tribunal to interfere. Held: The appellant failed to satisfy the Tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of power in this case was bona bonafide and was liable to be set aside as a bona fide exercise of his power under the Standing orders in this ease, because, as the employer wanted to take action for misconduct and then suddenly dropped the departmental proceedings which were intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r . 18 (b), it was now well settled that the employer can defend the actions under rs. 18(c) by adducing evidence before tribunal to prove that there Was in fact misconduct and, therefore,, the action was taken under a 'technical exercise of powers and was within the meaning of those Articles read with the rules framed under article 309 that questions relating to termination of service of government servants have to be considered. Sri Krishna Dalmia vs Shri Justice T. R. Tatachari, ; , referred to.

The appellants, who were lessees and sub lessees of the theatre, filed a suit against them for a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated November 27, 1954, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial Court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decision of the trial Court. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD : The order passed by the High court is set aside and the trial court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [436 A C] The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. 442 This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, , that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import; it includes civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Code to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial judge in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1, 1960, to be reopened, it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law. It is not open to any court of law to try an issue over again or reopen the same if an earlier decision operates as res judicata. Once the jurisdiction of the Court has been taken away, any proposal to reopen the question closed by the earlier decision would be exercise of Jurisdiction which is a 'Court subordinate to the High ' Court; and concluded "It is not correct to say that such a thing far as the agreement of November 27 was based on any of the issues.

The respondent, an officer of the Indian Air Force, was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Army and was on contract for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme under the ex military officials were appointed on Contract basis for a stipulated period which could have been extended fromtime to time and that the period of contract con firmed upto 30th August 1985 by an order passed in September, 1981, and it was again extended upto 31st March 1983 by an orde r dated 1st June, 1983. The terms of the officers mentioned under para 2 of the order of appointment issued on 20th August, 1979 were couched almost in the same language. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the said order includ ing the above term relating to the period for which he was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of Uttar Pradesh ' Thereafter, on 29th March, 1985 the service of the 1st respondent was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The order was to be effective from the date of receipt of termination order and no charges were men tioned therein against the 1 st respondent. The Respondent aggrieved by the said orders of termina tion filed a Writ Petition in the High Court. A Single Judge of the High court found that the order terminating that had been served on the respondent was an invalid one since it had been issued on the basis of Vigilance Report and no opportunity had been given to him to show cause why such action should not be taken against him. In the appeal to this Court by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (1) the order dated 1 6.1983 in the circumstances could not have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the competent au thority; and (2) since the interim ordi ned period allowed by the competent authority was without any notice having been given, the respondent had put forward at that stage such a case; and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to grant relief. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1(a) The appointment of the respondent is indisputably in the nature of contract and under the last order of appoint ment refened to above he was entitled to continue in office in the post in question till 30th of August, 1985 if the order Of termination of service served on him 29.3.1985 was found to be an invalid, one; and there was no order of extension of service. [242B C] (b) The order passed on Review of the Judgment dated 24.3 1988 does not make out that the respondent has put forward in at that Stage such a ease. His only case was that the interim order that had be passed on 10.7.86 entitled him to be reinstated in service even though there was an order of extention of service and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension.

The appellant was acquitted of an offence under Section 302, Indian Penal Code. The trial court found appellant guilty under section 302 IPC and sentenced him as also to suffer imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal mainly because another view is possible. The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thou ht that an order of discharge could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial, and compelling reason". [368C E] Sanwat Singh 's case may he added the further principle that "if two reasonable conclusions can be reached on the basis of the evidence on record, the Appellate Court should not disturb the finding Of the Trial Court." This, is not a new principle. It stems out of the fundamental principle, of our criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of any reasonable doubt. If two reasonably probable and evenly balanced views of the evidences are possible, one must necessarily concede the existence of a reasonable doubt". But, fanciful and remote possibilities must be left out of account. To entitle an accused person to the benefits of a doubt arising from the possibility of a duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him. If the preponderance of probability is all one way, a bare possibility of another view will not entitle the accused to claim the benefit Of any doubt. [368E F; 369A B] Sanav Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan , relied on.

The appellant who was an advocate in the Supreme Court, was convicted for having committed an offence of criminal misconduct under section 161 I.P.C., by the Chief Justice and a Judge of the High Court, whose conviction was confirmed by this Court, when the matter came up before it for hearing. The appellant contended that he was not given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge from his office, as required by Section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and that the President was given the power to appoint the Judges of the Supreme court as well of the said High Court. On behalf of the respondent it was urged that this power to punish a high Court judge only in article 124(5), clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 read with Article 2 18, was not applicable to the case of a Judge as provided under Article 124, clauses (1) and 4 of the Constitution for removal of the Judge. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The power to dismiss a High Court Judge or the Chief justice of a High Courts is a legislative one and Courts are regulatory in character and not judicial review which can properly be exercised in the exercise of their administrative powers which are not subject to any rules made by the executive authority. [234B C] 2.1 If the Act is applicable to judges of the high Court, then on his retirement the person from office cannot be prosecuted without sanction under Section 6, and therefore, the non possibility of previous sanction for prosecution under Section six would be sufficient to deal with the situation. [235F G] 3:2 The power of ap proached by clause (c) thereof is subject to the provisions of Article 246 read with article 248. Therefore, in respect of offences under Clauses (a), (d) and(e), the procedure for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [236E] 3.3 provisions of clause 1 and 2 of Article 123 read with Articles 124(4) to seek the prosecution of a judge or Chief Justice of a high court in case of appointment of a Judges other than the Chief Justices of the State and for the payment of salary etc., cannot be readily inferred. [237G] 4:3 The power under Article 246 is subject not to any limitation contained in article 77(2) nor can the power of judicial review be invoked in respect thereof, except by express or implied prohibition. In other words, if the holder of a public office while continuing in that office cannot not be prosecuted under this Act on account of his absence in sanction under Article 6, then, as held in Antulay, no sanction for his prosecution after ceases to hold the office may be necessary, but his prosecution is made because while in office he could be prosecuted with the previous sanction under section 6, he is not brought within the purview of the Act merely because Antulay decides that no sanction should be required for prosecution of such a Judge. [233D E] 5:4 The power conferred by clause(c) on the President by reason of Article 163 of the Constitu tion is subject only to the limitations envisaged therein. Therefore it is not necessary or expedient to prescribe any period for which any power can be delegated under that Article. [238E F] 4.5 Section 6 (1)(a) expressly enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 5 of this Act, alleged to have been committed by a public servant, except with the prior sanction, (b) in the case o f any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his Office. The President has not been given the exclusive or the sole intention of the Parliament or of the Legislature.

The respondent, a member of the Scheduled Caste, challenged the validity of the election on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal the appellant contended that he was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Castes group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appeared to have done, that there was no justification for doing that. After all, the evidence led in a case may be imperfect. Suppose the evidence, in another case led to the conclusion, as it might conceivably do do, that There was a smaller SC category within the Sunri caste of a person residing within the group of the Sunris. This is where the Tribunal went wrong and came to its conclusion that it had not been prov ed in this case that the appellant belonged to the smaller caste. [390G H] (2) The question now is, whether the respondent had established that the appel lant belonged to Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. To decide that point the description has first to be properly interpreted and understood, the Tribunal can ignore that construction of item 40 in the light of the evidence before it [390C F] (3) The expression "excluding Saha" meant excluding a smaller class group called Saha Sahas because the evidence on in the present case may conceivically do.

The appellant, a partner of Associated Commercial Enterprises, was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay which belonged to a lady named Durgeshwari Devi. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It was contended that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condition of the relin quishment by a tenant of his tenancy and whether in the present case there was no such relinquishment. Held, that an assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a wage owner is not made unlawful under section 15 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as it creates an offence and imposes a penalty of fine and imprisonment, and such sentence cannot be sustained. The words "relinquishment of his rights" in section 19(1) (a) of the Transfer of Property Act are "the relinquishment of his licen ture of any premises by a tenants. If by the expression, an assignment such as is to be liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligation under the tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason Of privity of Estate, the tenant ceases by virtue of privity of estate. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary; but in the case of relinquishment, it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them.

The respondent companies/appellants in Civil Appeal No. 2299 of 1979 were engaged by the appellants, for the purpose of earning annual increments. The workmen on their own behalf had been granted various benefits such as dearness allowance and house rent allowance. Some time later they were revised. There was no separate dearness allowance until January, 1977 when it was introduced for the first time, and a flat increase from 15 years to 20 years in the span fell due to change in the basic pay scale with flat increases. Two days after the award was made, an application was made by the Union stating: "In view of the increased in the dearness allowance, the increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in the category of Draftsmen and of Rs, 100/ to every employee in the other categories has been granted under my award. When the award is sent for publication, a necessary corrigendum be made in the award and the aforesaid words after figures Rs. 100 and Rs.100/ respectively have been added to the pay of each workman. The fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to this basic salary of every employee. One is the retrospectivity attached to the revised wage scales, and the other is the flat increased increase given to each individual workman. It was contended that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis, and that it would not be possible for the respondent to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the Unions for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in in the level of the basic wage. On appeal by special leave, it was contended: (1) The Tribunal erred in making the wage scales retrospective and in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January, 1976; (2) the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increased of Rs 150/ and Rs 100/ (3) that there would be a resultant increase in the Dearness Allowance and house Rent allowance. [179 B D] The Industrial Tribunal on a consideration of the material placed before it came to the conclusion that the company was in an undoubted position to bear additional financial liability. The question is to what extent the relief should be given to the employees ? If without any flat or ad hoc increase of salary, the workmen were to be fitted into the revised scales of pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. [173 F H] 2(a) It is well settled that a liberal approach, which is adopted by Courts will not necessarily interfere with an award unless some other method is adopted. The court will take care of the principal and the entire circumstances of each case particularly those where there are many employees who may have been allowed to exercise their powers under section 17(1) of the Act even after they had exercised their authority in terms of section 17A of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules. [174 A B] The decision of this Court in Tata Consulting Engineers first vs National Praxasi Mill Mazdoor Union ; distinguished. In the instant case, the Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellant and decided "to modify the existing structure of those scales with flat increase in each category". But it rejected the suggestion that a slab scheme should be introduced in the revising pay scale pertaining to different categories. The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal also does not reveal that there was any opposition by the company to the application for correcting the award.

The question arising in this appeal was whether the remuneration payable under an award was not already included in the definition of wages before the said definition was amended. Held, that since the Industrial Disputes Act provided for a new wage structure it did not affect the terms of contract between the parties till it was replaced by another contract. In construing the unamended definition of the term "wages" it is essential to bear in mind the scope and character of the powers conferred on industrial tribunals when they deal with industrial disputes under the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that although ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms Of contract between them, when they dealt with industrial dispute under the , Industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms thereof. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between tho parties, because that would be a fresh contract between two of the parties, and in this sense, was the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position in the matter is that when the industrial disputes are decided by a industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said award supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. This being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed by the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2(vi). Held also, that even though ordinary civil Courts which are not bound by an 'declared contract between parties when they dealing with industrial Disputes under the . Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act of 1958 had been amended in 1958 (the amendment was merely clarified what was included in "the unamended definition itself. The amendment has merely clarified certain what it was included and in the unamended term itself. In this connection, the South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, ; and V. B Godse, Manager, Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 (vi) to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudication, that this view is not well founded.

The appellant was a Sub division officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He had been charged under section 408 with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he was charged to his own residence. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him of that charge. On appeal by the State to the High Court it was discovered that the prosecution had not proved that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of the accused, and that though the thumb impression found in the acquittance roll was that of the appellant himself, he had included a fictitious name in the coverment Roll of the employee who had been employed. Held, that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting the appellant as it stood before a person could be prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. There was no difference in scope between that section and section 270 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and approving the statement of the law by Varadachariar, J. In the present case the elements alleged against the second accused were first that there was an 'entrustment ' and/or 'dphistic pleaders '; second, that the entrustment and/ or dominion was in his capacity as a public servant ', and third, that there could be no disposal, lawful or otherwise save by an act done or purporting to be done in an official capacity. The intention of sanction under s 197( 1) of Code of criminal Procedure cannot be doubted even if it was necessary to prosecute the appellant for want of sanction. But in view of this it was not necessary that a prosecution should be prosecuted for offences against a public servants on a charge of criminal misappropriation, will depend upon whether the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties attached (1) [1948] L.R 75 I.A. 185 and and therefore sanction was required under section 198(1).

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its income in British India as also in what is British India, but before 1939 it claimed to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the loss of Rs. 27,709 arose out of the business business and held that the banking business being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct losses incurred beyond Travancore State and in that respect disallowed a deductions on account of the loss from branches situate outside the Travancore State, because the assessee 's case had been specifically referred to the High Court. On appeal the Tribunal held that section 32(1) proviso fell in the second category and took the present cases out of section 32 (1) of the Travancore Income tax Act and awarded a sum of Rs., 79,275 on the loss in British country and other Indian States, but it was not answered by the High. In appeal to this Court, Held:(per Bose and Hidayatullah, jj.) : The object of the Indian Income tax Amendment Act is to allow set off of profits against losses arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 24 (1). But in the proviso to section section 24(1), which was to set off loss of profits or gains under one head against income, profits and gains under any other bead in any assessment year. There is no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business " and compel the application of the proviso by way of an addendum or dealing with a subject which was foreign to the main enactment. Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Madras; , distinguished. That section does not distinguish between business in British Indian India and business in an Indian State or so divide business. But then it was said that as the profits or losses of business in the two territories, i.e., British India there could be no deduction under one for all purposes as was the case under s.,10 which was intended to act according to its plain terms. It is a well settled rule of construction that a proviso must be considered with relation to the principal matter to which it stands as proviso. That apart, in a case where profits and losses arose under the same head they had to be adjusted against each other. Ltd. vs Commissioner Of Income tax Madras, [1951] section C. R., 295, relied on.

The first respondent held an All India concern in Bombay. In August, 1947 the company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The memorandum of Association provided that in respect of certain illness the clerical and subordinate staff were to retire its employees at the age of 55, subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. Subsequently, it was found that in several other States there was a general agreement that the age at 60 should be fixed at 60. The workmen claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he had completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal which held: (1) that in all the awards in recent times in Bombay region as regards the age was fixed at 55 or more; and (2) that the Bank may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (i) The Tribunal rightly held that the trend in Bombay Region had been to fix the retirement age at 55 but that it was not correct to say that the method adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with the matter of problem is not very commendable. [431 D] In the instant case, an attempt appears to have been made on behalf of the respondent Company to show that it is not correct and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal. Allowing the appeal with costs, Held:(i) On a consideration of all the materials placed on record, the Tribunal found nothing to justify any doubt about the correctness of what was stated on the earlier occasion. [427 E F] (ii) The award made by the Industrial Tribu nal directing that the date of retirement for workmen in all industries should be fix at 60 is bad. Setting aside the order fixing the age for the workmen of the respond ent company at 60, it is clear that on a close examination it is established that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend.

The appellants were the directors of M/s. T.T. T., and their employees in connection with the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 1 before us. While they were working as Inspectors for investigating the affairs, the appellant No, 2 was informed by its officers that the business of the company was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members and other persons who would be responsible for such irregularities and contravention. The first respondent issued a notice to the appellants alleging irregularities and even illegalities in the conduct of the appellants ' affairs to the Company Law Board Board. In September 1964 the first respondent passed an order on behalf of the Company, declaring that the affairs were being conducted by the company with intentto defraud its debtors, members, etc., and that it was not competent to issue any writ restraining the company Law Board and the Inspectors from giving effect to the order dated May 19, 1965. On April 2, 1965, the first appellant passed an ex parte order stating: " (1) that in making the said order the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b) of the ; (2) that the provisions of section 237 (b) were void as offending articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of The Companies (Amendment) Act, 1963 (Act No. 42 of 1965), read with section 642(1) clear and that the distribution of the work of the Board being merely a matter of procedure the order of the Chairman allocating the power under section 237 of the . Besides this there was ample material before the Board on which it could and did form the opinion that there were circumstances suggesting that as stated in the Order of May, 19, 1968, the business 'of the company had in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the Company and its members. " On April 3, 1965; the first Appellant passed an exparte order setting aside the ex parte orders dated April 2 and April 13, 1965 holding that the appellants were entitled to an order which was made mala fide. The second appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ directing the Board to give effect to its order dated April 19,1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The petition was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf Of the appellants (i) that section 237 contemplated only two things: (1 ) the opinion of the board and (2)(ii) the existence of circumstances suggesting one or more of the matters specified in sub cls. (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of section 10E. HELD: (i). The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 to order investigation and delegated by it to the company law Board was administrative that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman, Company Law Boards, and that if the grounds were disclosed by the Board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. In other words, the act of the chairman was in the nature of a fishing expedition and not after satisfaction that the funds of the companies were being carried on even prima facie with the intent to evade creditors, member and other person or persons concerned in the management of the affairs. The order dated 5, 1965 was passed by the first appel lant respondent ex parte without affording any opportunity of being heard; (ii) that there was no material before it to form the said opinion; (iii) that if grounds are disclosed by ' the Board, the Court could examine them; and (iv) the power conferred by section 236(b), was merely administrative: because no honest opinion was formed on the matters which under the section gave rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material material.

The appellants were convicted on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to them. They had approached the carts and pelted stones. The Police investigated the case and arrested the 20 persons who were accused in the case as being the culprits involved in this incident. On the application by the prosecution for a declaration that the appellants were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the present case, HELD : The proper inference was drawn in this case. There was no question of presumption. [14E] If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of stolen property with him was a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found. Since from each person a large number of goods the same type such as 20 choli pieces or ten pieces of paper were found, it was impossible to think that these 20 persons belonged merely receivers of stolen properties from some other 20 persons. The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. [15G H] It is reasonable therefore to raise the presumption in this ease that the accused were dacoits themselves. As regards the sentence, the offence no doubt was serious. But no injury beyond one appears to have caused. Therefore, a sentence of three years ' rigorous imprisonment will meet the ends of justice in this cases.

Rules of 1926 were made in exercise of the powers under the Act those list of substances were included in the said list and they are not hit by any limitation or unreasonableness. [233G H; 234A B] The provision of Sections 2(4) and section 5 are not violative by any consti tutional limitation. There is no compelling jus ties on any ground to exclude any requirement in the Rule, namely that any require ment in this Rule is unreasonable or offends the petitioners ' right to carry on trade or business.

[82 D] (2) The workmen were entitled to 7 days sick leave on full salary during the period of their physical incapacity, incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. The appellant 's fundamental right to be afforded a reasonable opportunity of making a representation under article 22(5) of the Constitution included two distinct components. (a) there was a sudden search by the police on the 24th August, 1954 at the appellant ' his place for alleged possession of illicit liquor and (b) an assault on himself (appellant) by a gang of persons of whom some were employees of the Dewas Action Committee. The activities which are being carried on by the appellant with the object of causing further deterioration in the relations between the Portuguese Government and the Indian Government over the question of devotion to India, were prejudicial to the security of India. The High Court held that there was no reason for disagreeing with the conclusion of the High Court on the ground that the material was not enough to make out that the detaining authority was acting otherwise than bona fide. Held: (i) In so far as the requirements of article 22 is concerned, it is now well settled that the obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining Authority not in any other manner. It is enough to say that there is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the detaining authorities at the time when grounds were furnished. (ii) The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to disclose him is subject to the limitation under article 19(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interests cannot be required. (iii) The requirement for such communication would depend on the circumstances of each case, as was pointed out by this Court in Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya vs State of Bombay, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 135. (iv) If any particular ground which is supplied is incapable of being understood or defined with sufficient certainty it can be called vague. The fact that the detenu himself does not appear to have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration.

There was an allegation of misconduct. The allegations were as follows: Rao was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Sectionundrabad. He was charged with gross misconduct. After a General Court Martial was constituted for the trial of the respondent and the order was set aside by his order dated September 4, 1958 removing the respondent from service. The respondent thereupon filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954 was ultra vires the , as the action taken thereunder was without any authority and therefore violative of section 45 of the , which he was not empowered to remove him from service in derogation of the provisions of section 28 of the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r, 14 was intra vires the . It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "subject to the provisions" occurring in section 19 make s.19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government had thus no power to remove a person from the service and that if this rule was ultra rites it must be said that r was not ultra vires and that the action took thereunder was neither without any jurisdiction nor was there any provision of law for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45 or for removal on his own account. The High court accordingly dismissed the writ petition holding: (i) r.14 was ultra vided by the provisions contained in Ch. VI of the Act and that as section 19 uses the words 'subject to . the provisions Of this Act ' , it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service '; and (ii) in absence of specific provision for punishment it was contended that there should be rules, and subject to the three provisions of the, Act that r came into force only after the trial. HELD : (i). The words " subject to this Act", occurring in s. 19 makes section 19 subject to s, 45, and the power under s.20 is an independent power. Although section 19, uses the word "subject tO the provisions . , it says of removal ,of a person at from the Service; it speaks only of removal and removal of such a person in the service. In the present case there was no doubt that r could not be challenged in this Court as it meant to give power to the Central Govern ment to remove an officer without being tried by a court martial. The two sections 19 and 45 were mutually exclusive. There was therefore no reason why the rule should have been issued for removing a person outside the service in violation of section 29 (2).

The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 31(1), read with section 33(1) of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250, The case against them was that they had terminated their services by sending two letters to the Conciliation Officer stating that no useful purpose would be served by holding any further meetings. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings had continued for more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952: Held, (i) The making of a report under section 12(6) of , on the report of an conciliation officer is not deemed to take place when the report is received by the appropriate Government, and even assuming that it was a case where no settlement was arrived at, he was to submit his report within 14 days but that did not affect the pendency of the conciliation proceeding. (ii) The provisions of section 12 which applied to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise, do not support this contention as the termination of the dispute was deemed to have taken place when it is received and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if the proceedings were not closed but were carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation officer did not make his report under that section he was guilty of breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days. The expression " pendency of any conciliation proceeding" given by section 12 must have been interpreted in workers of the industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the Industry Colliery, (1962) 2 S.C.R.

On the other hand, it was urged that the grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by section 2(2), detention order and public order. [955G] Harak Chand Banthria vs Union of lndia, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union Of India & Ors., [1962] Supp. 2 SCR 240 referred to.

The appellant, who had been granted a licence under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for the running the cinema theatre in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu in Collaboration with two osher persons, namely Todar Mal and Kishan Kumar. By another order dated April 21, 1979 a licence was issued by the Government to Ved Gupta in respect of the subject matter of the cinema. On September 26, 1980, the Superintendent of Police reported that cinema exhibition of cinematograph films in the Theatre may be suspended till March 31, 1970, provided that Shri Ved GUPTA or any person to whom with the consent of the licensing authority, the licence is transferred continues to own or manage the cinematographs used ill the said Apsar Theatre. The appellants were displaced persons on 30 8 1952. The respondent applied to the Custodian of Evacuee Property under section 12 of the , for a declaration that the lease dated December 1, 1951 was in respect of property belonging to the evacuee and that therefore they became vested in the respondent as the custodian for the State. One of the grounds taken by the appellants was that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section I9 of the Act. The Custodian rejected this contention and dismissed the application. An appeal filed against this decision was allowed by the High Court in revision, though it related to distinct matters which were not raised in the petition. In appeal before the Supreme Court, HELD: (i) Section 12 did not confer an authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. The operative portion of section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision in that section. [123 A, D] Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, applied for the contention that section 12 did no by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and cannot prevail as against them and has been inserted ex abundanti cautela. It is well settled that a non obstante clause applies to all other laws for the time being in force, and does not include "or any contract between the parties". Such an interpretation will defeat the object of the non obstante clauses of section 12. [124 A B] (ii) The section expressly authorises the custodian to vary the conditions of a lease, or vary, the terms of it thereto is unqualified, absolute and absolute, that power could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease is held.

The respondent Board of Revenue determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh. Later, on, the Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Sub Divisional Officer and remanded the case to the Sub divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the calling area for 300 Raghubir Singh, and after remanding the land to the sub divisional officer, Hanumagangarh in the light of the observations of the Board 's order dated 14th April, 1975, held that the land in possession of Raghubir Singh was ancestral. The Sub Divisional officer also ordered that the ceiling case initiated against the respondent should be transferred back to the Revenue Authority for further determination of this land. The appellant contended before the High Court that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers, as the High court had held that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955. This case has no application for interpretation of the present Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955. The contention on behalf of the appellant to that effect was negatived but on merits the High 's view that it was not appropriate for the Board to exercise the powers conferred by section 9 of the land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the Board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and Control and the order passed by the Board was set aside. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of superintendence vested in an all court and where interest of justice requires exercise of such powers. [728A] 2. Under section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ' but sub section (2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High .court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [325H; 325A] 3. The Board had by its order dated 30th July, 1975 directed that the Ceiling area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956 and not according to the new law i;e., Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973. [326E F] 4. Even if the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to the Board of revenue to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before the Rajasthan High Court in Kana and others vs Board of Reams & Ors., ; , referred to. [316A B] 5. Section 221 cannot be said to have been limited to the executive control and superintendence of the board over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th February, 1966 a fresh document of that date was executed and it is alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and license ' to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. Clause 2 of this agreement recites that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 till 31st August, 1970, that agreement was being executed. It is alleged by the licensor that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. This agreement was in writing and this was for a period of 5 years. The main contention involved in these proceedings was whether the appellant was the tenant or a licensee? The answer would he dependent upon the construction of the documents. It was also contended that the expression " licence" appearing in clause 2(1)(a) of the agreement recited that the licence had been given and granted 'leaves and Licence ' to the licensee to use. and occupy for the term of five year. In reply, it was stated that the appellant continued by virtue of that agreement. It would be evident from the document that it was a licence and not a licence. The Trial Court in the City Civil Court decreed the ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered eviction. Against the order of the trial court, an appeal was filed before the High Court which dismissed the same. In this appeal on special leave it was contended for the appellant that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was to be framed; and that even in any event by filing the application for eviction the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour, and that in any case it was recorded that as per clause 2 of the said agreement, the licensee would be entitled to keep the keys of the premises with him and shall be at liberty to work in the said Premises for twenty hours subject to restriction of rules and regulations imposed by the Municipal or any other local authority or authorities. It could not make any difference for the Court trying the issue as to whether the respondent was a sub tenant as such or not; that in view of the express provision contained in clause 15A(1) of section 16 of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the property as licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the 1st February, 1973. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. In order to go back to the findings of the Trial Court and the High Courts below, it is a licence which involves a transfer of interest in land, Subba Rao, J., who held that the period was of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. The High Court was not right in interfering with the finding of the Small Causes Court that the Respondent was a tenant and having found that the amount of rent, light bill stood in the name of the respondent showed that there was no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned hereinbefore and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. [1060 E] 2. It cannot be said that there is no equity in favour of the Respondent. [1012 A B] 3. The view taken by the High court or the Court of Small Causes was incorrect. In determining whether an agreement creates between the respondent the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. The United State of Rajasthan was formed by Covenant entered into by the Rulers of Rajasthan including those who had formed the former State of Rajpur and which came into existence with effect from April 7, 1949. Under cl. (2) all the assets and liabilities of the covenanting States became the assets of the new State of Matsya. The United State was formed under the Covenant by which the old States were merged in May 1949 and thus the former State of Dholpur came to be included in the United State Of Rajasthan through the Matsya Union. Thereafter, the United States of Rajasthan became the Part B State of India on January 26, 1950. [179 C] In view of this difference between a case where there was no recognition by the new sovereign and in that respect the present case, the old laws were to continue till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. [182 E F G] The fact that a merger took place the new state by a provision in the Covenant throughout would be valuable evidence from which affirmance of the rights mentioned therein could be inferred and added that such inference must relate to act or conduct of the old State after it came into force would not affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations. The distinction between a situation where an agreement was entered into in one way the other provided for the recognition by a new sovereign, the former was that of the former though it was made with reference to article 295(2) of the Covenant the latter agreed that the new States would continue in force in the State concerned subject to tile modification that reference therein to the Ruler or Government of Rajasthan shall be construed as a reference to the Rajpramukh or, as the case may be, to the Government of India. The second thing, however, was to hold that the old law must prevail and in the present ease there was recognition of liability by the respondent throughout this process of merger from 1948 to 1950. In view Of this difference when a new State continued all the old agreements till they came into being or altered it follows in our opinion that the rights arising under the old contracts in the subjects of the merges would continue and these subjects would have the same rights against the new con tract. In order to come to the conclusion that on continuing the old, laws, until they were altered or modified as a result of the continuance of the previous laws, whether there was an recognition by, the new power was given to the new territory throughout this course it is unnecessary to decide whether the particular words in article 295 Of the Covenant or similar provision throughout the process of these political changes. [183 B D] The present case was not one of such cases and neither of them applied to the Mills.

The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Act, 1933 and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (1) The contention that the provisions imposed by section 5 are not only unreasonable but tend to defeat the very purpose of the legislation was based upon a reasonable classification which could be reasonably justified as reasonable under the circumstances prevailing at the relevant time and the same has to be considered along with other considerations which cannot now be visualized. (2) The object of the Act is to protect the growers, the trade, in commercial crops, the standards that will be maintained in the present market at that time, the comparative merits of the existing market and the market to be built up and other relevant factors which cannot thereafter be visualised. [101 H] (3) It cannot be said that the decision Of this Court in Madras State, as in other parts of the country, provide for the better regulation of the buying and selling of commercial crops within the radius prescribed. But when a market is established no licence to purchase, or sell, commercial crops will be granted or renewed in respect of any place situated within such distance from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Government and that nothing under the Act prevents the Govern ment from fixing a long distance as a prohibited area. [10 E F] (4) The argument proceeds on the same footing that if the payment is made de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it would be a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the impugned Act. Trade involves exchange of commodities for money, the business of buying and sale of the trans ferers involves the seller, the buyer, the commodity sold and the price paid for the sale. Under the section if such payment is de hors its terms, but made as towards consideration, for the user of the Premises or services, it was not a deduction from the price or in any transaction.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. They contended that the conviction of the present appellants was illegal because they had been convicted in a previous case though they had not appealed; that when the eye witnesses arrived after it started, they began to attack the appellants with axes and sticks and threatened their, and then ran away; but there was nothing to indicate that they ran away together as a body or that they met afterwards. Held, that in order to bring home the guilt of the appellant, it must be shown that the accused had done anything except be present, and even if it be accepted that certain men could have known what happened, but none could be vicariously convicted for the act of any of the others; but when, appellate Judges who agree on the question of guilt differ on that of sentence, it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons. The fact that the injury caused death was the one would not necessarily lead to his inference in another case; Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs King Emperor, (1932) L.R 52 I.A. 45, relied on. In a case like that there could arise and be formed suddenly, as for example when one man calls on bystanders to help him kill a given individual and they both by their words or their acts indicate their assent to him and join him in the assault; it is not enough, as in the latter Privy Council Case, to have the same intention independently of each other, e.g., the intention to rescue another and if necessary to kill those who oppose. In the present case there was no evidence where a common intention embracing the accused could legitimately be inferred. If the prosecution cannot prove that his separate blow was a fatal one he can only be convicted for that act of others; and if the prosecution could not prove that their separate blow fell a conclusion of fact in another cases, it would not be proper to hold that there was an intention to kill such an offence. It was also settled that in any case the fact that some men had attacked the deceased with an axe only inflicted a light blow on the scalp which did not break any of his injuries could not take the common intention required by the section because there was, no prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan.

Dismissing the writ petition, this Court HELD: (1) Rule 56(j)(i) is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis i.e. in a Brosive capacity, and not on an officiating basis merely. [637C] (2) The determination of the competent authority under sub clause (i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class I or Class II service or Post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis and such officiation lasts for a number of years. Officiating promotion certainly does not confer a right to the post and at any time the Government servant may be sent back to his substantive post. [643D E] (3) Before a Government servant belonging to a Class I service or class II service/or post on regular basis has to be retired compulsorily, it is necessary for him to have a lien. [65C] F.R. 56 referred to. (4) It is clear from the language of sub clause(ii) that sub clause would also be applicable to all Government servants and sub cl.(i) carves out a class of government servants into a category and makes a special provision.[640B C] (5) Under sub clause 2, an officiating Govern ment servant does not really belong to Class I and Class II Service or post even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily oron arly or on ad hoc basis. [64D E; 644C D] (6) The intention of the rule is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire government servants in the public interest and that classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) has a purpose behind it.[645G F] (7) The decision in Tahiliani 's case was not correct.

One V had filled a proposal for insurance for Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. There was medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased on 27st December, 1960 and it was further stated that the said two cheques were encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated, the amount and credited in the accounts towards the premium payable by the deceased. The Divisional Manager, who was competent to accepting a proposal form for Rs 50, 000, rejected the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premium in full. As the proposal was not considered, the terms of acceptance were not fixed and the premium amount required for the proposal, was not calculated. Another cheque was encashed by the appellant on 29th December, 1961. The widow of the late deceased, respondent No. 1 herein wrote to the appellant intimating the death of the proposer and demanded payment of Rs.50,000. TheDivisional Manager denied liability on behalf of the Corporation on 28th January, 1961 contending that in this case the first Premium was not only received by the Corporation completely on 11th January; but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by respondent No 1 without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any. of sending communication of acceptance of proposal. The deceased had filled up a proposal and after setting out the facts which had been set out hereinbefore, that the medical examination report was submitted to the corporation with regard to the proposal as well as the preliminaries were completed and it, therefore, there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. On the question whether there was a concluded contract of insurance between the appellant and the respondent Corporation, the High Court took the view that the policy commenced on 11nd January, 1968 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the corporation; and that the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first premiums by the late husband of respondent No1 herein. The High Court accordingly allowed the appeal of respondent Nos. 1 & 2. Allowing the Appeal of respondent nos. 3 and dismissing the Civil Miscellaneous Petition filed against the judgment and order of the High court, this Court, HELD: (I) In the instant case there was clear admission to the effect that there was assurance on behalf by the field officer and local agent to the deceased that the payment of the first insurance would amount to the acceptance of the proposal. [353A] (2) When an insurance policy becomes effective is well settled by the authorities but before we note the said authorities, it may be stated that it is clear that the expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. (See in this connection the statement of law in Corpus Juris Secundum, Vol. XLV page 986 wherein it has been stated: "The mere receipt and retention of premiums until after the death or of applicant does not give rise to a contract, although the circumstances may be such that approval could be inferred from retention of the premium." [353H; 353A] MacGillivray & Parkington on Insurance Law, Seventh Edition p. 1267.)

A dispute relating to a civil proceeding was referred for adjudication in a suit under the provisions of the Act. The trial court held that an order granting interim injunction did not determine the rights of the parties within the meaning of article 134(1)(c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint was pending, was whether the order granting an ex communication was invalid. Held, that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights and liabilities of the par ties is not a 'final order ' within the" meaning of Art 133(1) (c). [704 F; 704 B] The orders passed by the High Court in appeal which did not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding, were therefore 'a final one and not appealable to the judicial Committee. This was not a final order within the ' meaning of that article and the term "final order" occurring in Article 133( 1) must be understood in its ordinary sense so as to include an order passed by a court which maintained the order of the Court of first instance or proceeding and leave it the rights in disputes have to be determined, the order is interlocutory. Abdul Rahman vs D.K. Cassim & Sons, , relied on. The orders now under appeal do not finally disposed of those rights but leave them to be determine by the courts in the ordinary way. " In the instant case no final order had been passed and it was not contended that the order was final within the terms of article 133(I)(c).

Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabil ities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at that, is sold by the processor. Rule 174 enjoins that whenever goods owned on job work basis, will leave the processor 's Factory plus his profits. The Department has relied upon Note added by the Tribunal for determining the assessable liability of the appellants to pay excise duty in respect of their goods cleared under Rule 174(1) but not the separately determined value.

The assessee, a religious teacher, filed a suit claiming that the property belonged to the Math Sauna or deity of the deity. The High Court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment, that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math. In appeal by special leave, the appellant urged: (i) there can be no presumption either way; and in each case the burden is upon the plaintiff to establish that the properties in respect of which he is asking for possession are property to the possession of which the assessee is entitled. (ii) There could be no proof either way. All the facts and circumstance must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to the math or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. In the present case there was no presumption by either way or the other at all. The fact that a Mohunt was an ascetic does not raise any presumption that a property in his possession is not his 's personal property. Strictly speaking, there is no presumption in either way and in every case the onus is on the plaintiff in establishing that the specified properties are those properties to the posses sion of which it is entitled in the right in which he sues. [663G H] In the instant case, there was an assessment proceedings under the U. P.
