An advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof successful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the previous written examination was not called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry it was factually estab lished, the Public Service Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examina t tion and asked for re holding of it. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. Whenever no defect is pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the viva voce examination from the interview. there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examinati tion and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that there was disinclined for reing the written parts of the recruits examina te and the only objection was restricted to exclusion. [ 126 F] 2.

The plaintiff appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. Som Dass, the defendant, contended that the property belonged exclusively to the D becha or its properties, that when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant decree was reversed and the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass his erstwhile mahant had the right to manage the properties of the dera at Land Seke, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant of the primary Dera; that the appellant had no right to recover possession of such property of the If he was not impleaded within the period prescribed as he claimed to represent the dera as its duly elected Chela. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that there had been no devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit on death of a previous mahant by virtue of law or custom that there would be devolution of interest in that subject matter on the death, of a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahant and when a dispute is raised regarding such rights then the plaintiff was bound under Order 22 rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired; and that the appeal could be continued under O. 22 r. 10 after the demise of Som Chand Dass, since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahants against the original mahant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant, [489 A] 3. The appellant had raised an alternative contention before the High court that there 'was no abatement of the appeal even if Som Dass were not impleaded in within the prescribed time as he contended to represent it. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of his interest during the pendency of a suit, and new persons are elected to fill their place, it is a case of devolution of 'interest during the course of a trial and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 2 22, r.10 notwithstanding that such period of time for impleading themselves had expired. [489 C F] 4. The appeal could not be continued against the defendant appellant in his absence, since he was an unsuccessful person to represent him. [490 C D] 5.

The Andhra Pradesh State Government ordered reduction of the age of retirement from 58 to 55 years on the ground that it had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths in order to improve the lot of the common man, and that the employees were stagnated in the lower positions due to increase in the age. On February 8, 1983 an order was passed by the Government stating that it decided to reduce the age Of superannuation from 58 and to 55, that the said recommendation was accepted by the State Government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect from October 29, 1979. The petitioners challenged the validity of Rules 148 (3) and 149(3) of the Civil Services (Classification Control and Appeal ) Rules, 1966 which were amended later. It was contended on their behalf that there was no basis at all for reducing the age retirement of Government employees; that the question of the 'age of superannuation was not referred to the Commission and that it could be taken away if at all only from future entrants to the Government service; and that even the introduction of Amendment Rules with retrospective effect by Amendment Rules was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD : 1. The provisions of the Ordinance which are sought to be amended retrospectively, are violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution for the following reasons: (a) The impugned action of the State in reducing the retirement age of government employees was not based on any recommendation of the Commission; (b) the question whether the Regulations imposed a discrimination on the petitioners by restricting their conditions of service, could be challenged as lacking in authority. [587B] 2.1 It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended, since they can be made, under the proviso to Article 309 and that, the power to amend these Rules carries with it the power, to amend them retrospectively. Therefore, the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of powers conferred by Article 309, by which the proviso of Rule 2 was deleted retrospectively, is a valid exercise of legislative power. [588C] 3. The impugned orders are liable to be struck down. In the instant case, there is no basis for the contention that the amendment to the Rule was beyond their powers. [58D E] 4. The State Government had reviewed the situation arising out of the enhancement of the retirement from 55 to 58 years and that though it was earlier increased from 55 years to 58, the general trend was for reducing age of superannuation.

The appellants are dealers in the State of Haryana. He purchased certain raw materials inside the State for sale without paying tax thereon, in view of the provisions contained in section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The department alleged that the sales effected by the appel lants were not sales in the course of export outside India within the meaning of Section 5(1) of the Act. The assessees however, denied the relief on the short ground that the goods were not sale in the ' promotion year 's account. The sales effected were inter State sales chargeable under section 5(2) and not under section 6 or section 24(3). The assessees filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of section 9(1)(a)(ii) on the ground: (i) that section 9 (1) exempts only sales made in the offi cits failing under sub section (3) and those failing under subsection (1), therefore, there could be no levy of purchase tax under section 9. The High Court dismissed all the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Except for certain reasons, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (a) Section 9(i)(b) does not exempt only sales from tax which are exempt even if purchased by a registered dealer for the purpose of export within the State but also those falling under sub s.(1) and (ii) that as the sale effected by them fall within one of the three exempted categories set out in section 9, there can be no con struction of purchase Tax under section 49. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD : 1. The definition of 'turnover ' in Section 2(c) would include only sales falling within the scope of section 5 (1). Clause 9(21)(b), as it stood prior to its amendment by Act i/s. I.O. 47 of 1976, uses the words "within the meaning o sub section" of section " have to be given full meaning; in other words, the exemption under section 10 has to be restricted only to export sales falling outside the scope Of section 5. Clause 9 (21)(a) refers to cases where raw materials are purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section 2(e) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the 361 State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in tho course of inter state trade or commerce.

The respondents sold to dealers certain goods which were shipped by the buyers. The sales tax authorities assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the purchase of castor oil which they later sold for the sum of Rs. 6,47,5091,6 as mentioned above. In appeal it was contended that they remained their property till they crossed the customs barrier and therefore could not be taxed. Held: (i) The goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought on board at the time the export was not postponed even after shipment. The intention of the parties that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of Imports & Exports (Control) Order, 1954, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the point of time when they cross the customs frontier was crossed and that in case such despatch outside the State of Bombay was by a person to whom the certifying dealer has sold the goods but who is not a registered dealer it cannot strictly be said that the declaration has not been carried out. (ii) The scheme of the Legislature clearly is that where the intention as declared has not fulfilled, purchase tax should be levied. Per section Bornimmal, J. (dissenting) (i). The words " a person " in section 10 (b) must be interpreted to mean a person who has given such certificate under section 8(b), and the declaration thus made is intended for being despatched by him or by a registereddealer to whom he sells them to an address outside the state of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase. In other words, in the context where the testator clearly declared that the goods were intended for use " in the customs country it would not mean nothing more than that the property in the goods should pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial waters of the country, or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. Whichever view is taken there was nothing to indicate that the intention to comply with the requirement of el. 5 (2) Of the Imports & Export (Control ) Order carries with it an intention that the vehicle should pass to the buyer at the place of the goods cross the Customs barrier. The scheme clearly implies that where sale has been effected. purchase tax would be levied only if the goods are not 'despatched outside the customs limits of the State or at a later date when the place leaves the Port: Whic whichever view is given there was something to indicate, that the intended intention to do and to agree as between themselves that the commodity in the thing shall pass immediately thereafter before the contract goes beyond its territorial waters. Where the intention is declared by the purchasing dealer under section 7 of the Imports (Control)(Control) Act it will be in the normal course of export commences at the port of export and not after shipment, and since the time of the export commences for the purpose of article 286(1)(b) it was for the sellers to obtain the necessary licence. If such despatch along the State is by a dealer to whom goods are sent outside the States, the purchasing dealers may not be liable for having made a false declaration ". The mere fact remains that the object declared has been not carried out and purchase tax could not therefore be held to have commenced till the ship had passed beyond the local limits. (iii)The onus of proving that it is a 'regarding intention of goods being despatched outside the Sate of Bombay should be on the seller.

The respondent husband married the appellant. In 1956, the appellant was divorced by his wife. The appellant 's mother and the respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. The compromise terms were settled in respect of the flat. For some time there was flickering improvement in relations between the quondum husband and the quodum wife and they lived together. Thereafter, again, the respondent separated became entranged. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant is a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her child and Rs 400/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) and (3)(b) which provides that a woman who has been divorced by her husband and that she has received, whether before or after the date of the said order, the whole of the sum which under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties, was payable on such divorce cancel, and (2) in any other case from the date on which such order was made. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(1)(a) The dominant purpose of the payment 'under any customary law or personal Law ' must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [78A] (b). The compulsive conclusion from a divorce by a husband and his provision of a separate residence as evidenced by the consent decree fills the bill. Do divorcees have to 1) prove mutual consent to live apart; Divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born, it is section 127(3)(bb) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of payment ' under any custom or personallaw ' must he to obviate the destitutionof the divorceee and to providing her with Wherewithalto maintain herself, the entire scheme of section 127 (3) (b), is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. To interpret otherwise is to stultify the project. Law is dynamic and its meaning cannot he pedantic but purposeful. The principle, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 127)(3)(B) absolution from this obligation under section 125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary orpersonal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [79G H] 1.(2) The compulsial conclusion from the divorce by the husband and its provision of separate residence was that Parliament intended divorcees should not derive a double benefit. If the first payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 126 not mathematically but fairly then section 127, (3), subserves a goal and cum appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof. [81F G] 3. A combined reading of the sub section and section makes it clear that ,the scheme of the complex of provisions in Chapter IX has a social purpose, and its benefit cannot be defeated if the first payments by way emption are within the cognisance of that provision.[82A ] 4.

An order of the Collector was challenged by a person who had secured higher marks in a public auction and the matter was referred to the Collector under section 35 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1955. The Collector dismissed the petition holding that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Aggrieved, the appellant filed an appeal before the Collector contending inter alia that there is no requirement specified in the Rule and the respondent was right. The Tribunal set aside the order and directed that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect of future contracts under the Collector is set aside. In this appeal on behalf of the State it was submitted that there has been no requirement and there is a clear clause in the Rules that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellant in respect future contracts, cannot be sustained in law. [867A B] 1.2 An implied principle of the rule is of the law that any person affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion is setaside. [869C D] PG NO 869 PG NO 837 PG NO 860 2.3 The last paragraph in so insofar as it directed black listing cannot be held to be a elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by an order should not have right to open and making representation against the orders.

The appellants were the landlords of certain premises. They leased out their properties under two lease deeds in favour of M/s. India Automobiles, which was then a property comprising an area of 4 grounds and 151 square feet with certain buildings thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953, all the co owners of the property (includ ing G.G.) sold the same to the United India Life Assur ance Company and the New Guardian of India Life Insurance Co. Ltd., which was later converted subsequently into a partnership concern of G. G. and his four sons. The firm and its partners are compendiously referred as 'the tenants '. The first lease deed (Ext. P 1) was dated 22.9.1947 and related to Door No. 2 (Item No.1 in Schedule A to the plaint). This was a property comprise of an area which was originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and measuring 41 grounds and 2005 sq. The lease deed provided that all the sub owners of this property (including G.L.) sold them to the Corporation, but subsequently, in 1961, the Life Insurance Corporation moved two applications (being HRC No. 3310) and 3311 of 1965) in the Court of the Rent Controller (Sri A. Varadarajan who later became a Judge of the said court) for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1 on the ground that they had not constructed any of the buildings thereon, nor had they constructed any new building thereupon. The said applications were allowed by an order dated 25.6.1954, and the Court held that the parties were tenants of the entire property covered by the lease deed and that they did not constructed the premises thereupon. It further held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Board had no jurisdiction to fix the fair rent; and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent En quiry Order in respect thereof had to fail.

The petitioner, who had retired as a respondent before the High Court, was given notice to submit his objections in respect of the preliminary list. The petitioner filed an affidavit and showed that the provisional gradation list was provisional. However, the legal position obtaining on such provisional seniority list was not prepared after hearing objections. The High Court held that the case now before this court is also governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court dismissing it was, HELD: 1.1 The combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962 so far as category 6 is concerned is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [ 828B C] Shankari vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , 224; Shri Bhagwan & Anr. vs Ramchand & Ant., ; , 222, referred to. 1.2 The combined provisional gradation List dated April 4, 1962 is ultra vided and illegal. [827F G] 1.3 In the instant case since no such opportunity was furnished to the respondents with regard to those two matters, they were bound by the provisions of the Act. [829G] Shankhadkar & Ors. vs R.D. Nanjiah; , ; 2.1 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, this Court is of the view that a Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. [828C] 1:2 The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard t he two points urged by the petitioner before the final gradation lists, being published and published as a final list. A right to represent was recognised as existing at time when the list was still to be considered as not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points. Clearly what was meant was that the publication gave the list finality. In that particular case, the fist had been prepared without due regard to the particular important point which had to he considered before finalisation. What has observed does not mean that if a final List is prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list is absent, it would still be inviolable ,Dr sacrosanct.

% It was common ground that the petitioners were granted Additional Licences under Import & Export Policy 1978 79 in Para 176 of the Import & export Policy for the period April, 1988 to March, 1991 to March 1991. In para 215 of the said Policy it was laid down that the import concession shall be limited by 10% of the gross foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made in preceding three licensing years termed as 'the Base Period '. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licences. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that the two petitioners had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78 whereas under Import and Export Policy 1988 91 they were entitled to import all other items whether canalised or otherwise in accordance with the relevant rules. These licences were valid for a period of 12 months and they contained the following endorsement: "This licence in valid for import of items permissible to Export Houses under the Additional Licence category as per Para 176, of Import Policy 1988 88, but are now covered by Appendix 1 Part B of this Policy. The Central Government rejected these applications on the ground that these petitioners had not diversified their export and that they had failed in diversification their export during the period 1977 78. The order refusing Export Certificate was challenged before the Bombay High Court by one of those writ petitions (filed by the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 460 of 1988) which was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court, and while the said appeal and other writ petition were pending in the High Courts, this Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1423 of 1984, Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, decided on April 18, 1985 wherein it was observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant/ entitlement of Export Houses in the Import and export Policy 1988 92. The Writ Petition and the appeal were heard together by a learned Single Judge. While dealing with the two petitions under Article 32 filed by the appellants against the order refusing the Export Certificate, this court made it clear that this Court has held that the grantees of the Additional licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy and that the word 'banned ' was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are `non canalised ' and also item which are 'canalised ' could not be ruled out.

Section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 provides that where the goods are delivered at the time of removal in a packed condition, including the cost of such packing except where the packing is of durable nature and is returnable by the buyer to the assessee, the value or the cost thereof, shall be included in the assessable value. Under section 4(5)(d), "value" in relation to any excisable goods, means (a) where thegoods are delivered in packed condition includes the cost for such packing, except the cost cost of the packing which is of a durable character and is served by the assessee to the buyer; and (b) wherethe goods are booked at the factory gate in a certain packed condition whatever may be the reason for such pack ing, the cost or the price of such wrapper or container or drum must be included In the assessable 'value" under section 4 (4)(D)(i), the cost shall be added to the price except where there is an agreement by the parties to the agreement. The appellant, a division of McDowell & Co., Ltd. was manufacturing and selling fusel oil/Styrene Monomer failing under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. In the said price lists, which were duly approved by Asstt. Collector, a reasonable rate of excise duty was charged on the goods manufactured by the appellant. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil/S eltyreneMonomer manufac tured by it was sold in bulk and delivered to the customers at the appellants ' factory. The said casel oil was a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture, it was stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the price lists were duly con cerned by the Asstt. Collec tor, the appellant had shown the value of fusel oils/Setyrene M Charterer manuufac lured by the appellants at the rate at which those were sold in wholesale as "naked Ex Works and in bulk". According to them, the manufacture of fuels oil was complete and it was the fully manufactured fusel on behalf of the appel lant. The question whether the cost o clause should be included for the purpose of assessment of excise duties, was answered against the appellant by the Tribunal holding that at the relevant time, the quantity of fu bail/Stiru steel tubes were not returnable by it and therefore, according to the appellant, it is not necessary for the said ca tions oil/styrene. The appeal filed by the Revenue before this Court against the decision of the Tribunal was also dismissed. Allowing the appeal of the Department, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It would create an absurd situation if durable packing supplied by the customer and returnable to the asses see is not to be included within the assessable price but a duisable packing supplied at the customer 's factory gate, which can be in cluded in the assessment value of the excisable goods where such goods are deliver at the place of removal, in packed conditions. If on the other hand, the manufacturer asks the customer to bring his own container and does not charge anything therefore, then the cost (or value) of packing cannot be 'notionally" added to, or subtracted from, the price at which the goods have been sold by the manufacturer.

The respondent Company was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport. On May 21, 1974, it wrote to the company requesting him to permit him to continue to live in the Company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement i.e. for 6 months; undertaking to vacate the flat as early as possible. It appears that the Company on humanitarian grounds acceded to this request and permitted the respondent to stay on in the company 's flat for six months after his option was available. However, he did not vacate the premises till August 27, 1987 when he addressed a letter requesting the Company to permit the appellant to continue for live in its premises during that period. In August 1986 the company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Estate officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the respondent Company and directed him to give a personal hearing to the respondent. Instead of availing of the said opportunity the appellant moved the High Court by a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High court which allowed the same set aside the eviction order and directed the Estate Officer to give only a personal Hearing to the petitioner. The company ' hereinbefore filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the Act, and the High Courts were in error in directing the Estate officer to give him a personal opportunity of being heard to the appellant. In view of the conflicting decisions of this court, the High courts ordered eviction of all the officers and employees who had been inducted into the flat and the premises alone should be evicted from the possession of the company. Against the order of eviction the petitioner filed a special leave petition before this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provision contained in section 630 of the H 172 is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to strict construction and there is no room for intendment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The terms 'officer or employee ' appearing in sub Section (1) of section 630 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employee of a company but also to include past officers and Employees of a Company during the course of their employment. [175G] 2. When the framers of the law in their wisdom thought it proper to bring within the mischief of the provisions of the act former officers or employees of a 'Company, they did not hesitate to do so and they expressly legislated. The High Court was therefore in error by striking down that provision. It is quite evident from clause (a) and (b) of sub section (1 ) of section 642 which defeats the very purpose and object with which it had been introduced. The appellant 's ancestors installed a temple in Amalner. The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. Though the origin of the Sansthan is dipped somewhat in antiquity and direct testimony was lacking, it has never been disputed that Sakharam Maharaj constructed a temple on the land at Amalningner. He also acquired certain properties and the said temple with the properties constituted Shri Vithal Shikhamai Sansthan of Amalantner. After the passing of Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 (Act 29 of 1950), an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons, who were Narayanrao Chimanrao Deshmukh, as constituted attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as the "owner" of the property. The word 'Buwa ' means a place by whatever designation known and used as a place of public religious worship. This evidence of Ramkrishna Deshpande stood corroborated by the Sanad which showed that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the ad trustee who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the properties. The appellant drew its attention to certain recitals in the deed of nomination executed by three businessmen of Ambalalner and held that the Sansthan was a public temple within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act, and as such it was a private property and not a public trust. Hence the application. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that: (1) there was absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the temple as a matter of right; (2) The High Court erred in holding that the temple was a 'private property and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as his own property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) There is absolutely no material on record to show that although Sakharamkar Maharaj, the founder of the endowment, had departed in the past century, and hence the dedication was in favour of the idol itself, and the point for decision was whether it was private or public endowment. [526C] The expression "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour Of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour by an individual as private property. [525D E] (ii) There can be no doubt that the beneficiaries of the deeds are the deity and the Sansthan and the gifts were made with the object of maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole.

The assessee, who was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Sales and Service Co., was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 52 by the Third Income tax Officer, C 1 Ward Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The grounds urged by the assessee were (a) that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act under which the Income Tax Officer issued a recovery certificate was void under article 13(1) as it offends article 14 Of the Constitution; (b) that Section 13 of Bombay City Revenue Land Revenue April, 1951 barred discrimination inasmuch as section 13(2), which sanctions such discrimination is clearly violative of the equal protection clause of the Constitution and has a statutory force and that the order of arrest was void in view of article 13 (1). Held: (i) The tax demand being a Union demand there should be uniformity in the punishment to be meted out to defaulters and it can be done easily by suitably amending section 46 (2), so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all states. The law was not dead; (ii) the law challenged before this Court has only adopted for its own purpose, the same coercive process which was devised by the States for their own purposes which were closely akin or similar to the purpose of the Union; and (iii) the position was different as it had to the object of the different Public Demands Recovery Acts. The statute provides for two different kinds of procedure for recovery of arrears of land revenue according as, the defaulter resides in the City of Bombay or in any other area within the State of Bombay. Section 13 does not purport to create a new class of persons but merely lays down that machinery is not incorporated in section 46 of the Act so as it can give an additional power on the Collector for the better and more effective application of the only mode of recovery authorised by the body of sub section (2) Of section 46. The Court cannot be called upon to decide whether the statute should be interpreted or applied. Having regard to the fundamental rights and contentions, it was not necessary to consider the question of its maintainability, after the dismissal of the petition under article 226 or to make any pronouncement on this occasion on the scope and ambit of Article 32 of the constitution in that situation. The discrimination complained of is not unconstitutional for the simple reason that the impugned law is based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. The provisions contained in section 13 would indicate at once that the procedure prescribed by section 13 was set out in the Indian Incometax tax Act, and it tells the Collectors of all other States to adopt the procedure laid down by their own State laws as if the provisions prescribing that procedure were set out therein in that section. The Legislature had not been directed to adopt a machinery which differs from State to State so that defaulters are treated differently in different states.

The respondents in this appeal are the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The dispute in the present case was a narrow one and whether the fixing of a two hours ' rest and two hours " overtime" involves a breach of the two sections. In so far as the question to be decided is when an employee works in an employment for more than nine hours on any day or for more exceeding forty eight hours in any week, he shall pay him for every hour at intervals of not less than four hours before he has an interval for rest of at least half an hour. The workmen claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shifts with 8 hours ' work overtime should be at least 3 hours if not 4 and by fixing only two hours of rest, each shift system would be introduced. The Workmen ' Union denied all the allegations but contended that the break up of a 12 hours ' shift into 8 hours had no application to it because the rate of duty in the opinion of the Trustees did not justify the change. The Union also contended that since the number of actual work hours was 48 hours per day for 6 days and a few times at the end depending on tides or the exigencies of the work, the case of the workmen could not be compared with that of the crew at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks and the latter could not therefore be compared. The employees claimed that the difference in the number between intervals of rest and hours must always include intervals of 7 days in a day and therefore, the period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at which the right had been worked in relation to wages. The contention that a 12 hour ' shift should be divided into 8 hour ' work and not a half hour must always included intervals of all rest, as that would justify the alteration. HELD: (i) The law of strike is founded on a distinction between the number and time of work at which, according to the ordinary working day, are to be performed. [629 A] (ii) In the present ease the workmen claim that under the scheme of 9hour shift from 8 hours to 9 hours ' overtime should not exceed 48 hours, though on any particular day the hours of work in a year may go up to 9. The provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3) give us an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest.

On 18th June 1948, the appellant was a thika tenant of a premises situated at Calcutta, which had been in arrears. On 18th July, 1948, appellant filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The first two defendants were described as thika tenants under the plaintiff and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on land and the tenancy right therein. In the plaint itself the second two defendants described as "thika tenant" as a tenant. No claim was made for rents or taxes although it was alleged that the same were in arrears, but no claim was raised for rents, taxes though it was contended by the third defendant who filed a Written Statement contending that he was a ' thika tenancy ' and not an 'khahara land ' as defined under that Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant took advantage of s.29 civil courts became unable to remit ejectment suits to the controller with the result that the Act as finally amended could not apply to pre licensing suits and thika lands. Before the Subordinate Judge a point was taken on behalf of the landlord that after the coming into force of the Act of 1949, the Rent Controller alone had jurisdiction in respect of ejectment cases as the tenant appellant was the 'a thikatenant ' within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended by the Act Of 1953. The Subordinate Judge held that at the time when the appeal of the defendant was disposed of by the Subordinate judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1945 and the definition of ' th February tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a revision filed by the respondent, the High Court held that sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre existing proceedings, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. In appeal to this Court the appellant contended: (i) that with the omission of section 28(b), the scope and ambit of those provisions must be considered properly; (ii) that even if a suit had been filed before the Act but was riot disposed of, by that date, the respondent landlord had acted on a notice under section 4 to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Ceiling Act, 1949, as amended upto 1953, and therefore, there was no question of any violation of sections 4 & 5 of the West Bengal Thika Revenue Act; (iii) the appellant having been given notice under s.4, he could not claim to eject his tenant in view of the vague definition in section 2 of the Bombay Thika Rent Act, 1950 as amended up to 1953, (iv) that the eviction decree passed by the appellate court must be affirmed; and (v) that section 28 was applicable only if the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the amendment of the definition. HELD: The protection under section 28 of the 1949 Act is available only to suits and proceedings which were pending at the date when the commencement of this Act, i.e., 21st October 1952. [179 C] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred followed.

Held, that the notice dated 13th March 1951, falls under the second Proviso and was valid.
